explanations.explanation: Right on the money, baker. The Servant says, "Listen to Me, O islands; pay attention, O distant peoples" (Isaiah 49:1). He isn't whispering to the folks next door. He's calling to people way out past the horizon, and I love a speaker who thinks that big.

Not quite, friend. No priests show up in this opening call. The Servant says, "Listen to Me, O islands; pay attention, O distant peoples" (Isaiah 49:1). He's reaching way past Jerusalem, and I think that's the whole surprise.

Babylon never gets named in this call, baker. The Servant says, "Listen to Me, O islands; pay attention, O distant peoples" (Isaiah 49:1). Kings do show up later in the passage, but they're watching the Servant, not the ones being called. The first call goes to far-off places, and that's a big mailing list.

That's the one, baker. The Servant says, "He made Me like a polished arrow; He hid Me in His quiver" (Isaiah 49:2). A quiver is the case that holds arrows, so this arrow is tucked away close. Polished AND tucked in. That's a well-kept arrow.

Close to a campsite, but no tent here, friend. The text says, "He made Me like a polished arrow; He hid Me in His quiver" (Isaiah 49:2). A quiver is what holds arrows. An arrow in a tent would just be a very confused arrow.

No tower in this verse, baker. The Servant says, "He made Me like a polished arrow; He hid Me in His quiver" (Isaiah 49:2). The quiver is the case that holds the arrows. An arrow in a tower sounds like a lot of stairs.

Yes, baker! The LORD says to Him, "You are My Servant, Israel, in whom I will display My glory" (Isaiah 49:3). The LORD says He will display His glory in this Servant. That's a mighty big thing to be told.

This one is actually true, friend. The LORD says to the Servant, "You are My Servant, Israel, in whom I will display My glory" (Isaiah 49:3). So the LORD says His glory will be displayed in Him. It's easy to second-guess a line like that, but the verse says it plainly.

Yes, baker! Even in the middle of that hard moment, the Servant says, "yet My vindication is with the LORD, and My reward is with My God" (Isaiah 49:4). Notice the "yet." He's worn out, but he doesn't stop there. He says where the reward is.

That's a natural guess, friend, but the verse points somewhere else. The Servant says, "yet My vindication is with the LORD, and My reward is with My God" (Isaiah 49:4). His reward isn't with people. It's with God, and that's a much safer place to keep it.

No king in this line, baker. The Servant says, "yet My vindication is with the LORD, and My reward is with My God" (Isaiah 49:4). Even after saying His labor felt like it was in vain, He puts His reward in God's hands.

explanations.answer: He is honored in the LORD's sight
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker! The Servant says, "for I am honored in the sight of the LORD, and My God is My strength" (Isaiah 49:5). This comes right after He talked about feeling worn out. Honored by the LORD AND strengthened by Him. That's a good place to stand.

explanations.answer: He is a stranger to the LORD
explanations.explanation: Not a stranger, friend. The Servant says the LORD formed Him from the womb to be His Servant (Isaiah 49:5). He also says, "I am honored in the sight of the LORD." You don't form a stranger from the womb.

explanations.answer: He is out of the LORD's favor
explanations.explanation: Nope, baker, it's the opposite. The Servant says, "I am honored in the sight of the LORD, and My God is My strength" (Isaiah 49:5). That's no one out of favor. I think it's a comfort after all that talk of laboring in vain.

You got it, baker! The LORD says, "I will also make You a light for the nations, to bring My salvation to the ends of the earth" (Isaiah 49:6). The job grows past Jacob's tribes and reaches the ends of the earth. That's one big light.

Not a king in Jerusalem, friend. The LORD says, "I will also make You a light for the nations, to bring My salvation to the ends of the earth" (Isaiah 49:6). Jerusalem doesn't come up in this verse. The light is for the nations.

No priest and no temple in this verse, baker. The LORD says, "I will also make You a light for the nations, to bring My salvation to the ends of the earth" (Isaiah 49:6). The job is bigger than one building. It reaches the ends of the earth.

That's right, baker! The LORD says, "Kings will see You and rise, and princes will bow down" (Isaiah 49:7). Remember who He's talking to: the One who was despised and abhorred by the nation. Kings standing up and princes bowing is a big turn.

That would be a different ending, friend. The LORD says, "Kings will see You and rise, and princes will bow down" (Isaiah 49:7). The Servant was despised and abhorred by the nation, and still the princes bow instead of turning away.
Not standing back, baker. The LORD says, "Kings will see You and rise, and princes will bow down" (Isaiah 49:7). The kings rise, and the princes bow. Nobody in this verse is keeping their distance.

No army in this verse, baker. The LORD says kings will see Him and rise, and princes will bow down "because of the LORD, who is faithful, the Holy One of Israel, who has chosen You" (Isaiah 49:7). The reason is the LORD, who is faithful and who has chosen Him. Nothing about a great army.

Right, baker. The verse says kings and princes honor Him "because of the LORD, who is faithful, the Holy One of Israel, who has chosen You" (Isaiah 49:7). No army is mentioned. It all comes from the LORD who chose Him, and that's a good reason to bow.

Yes, baker! The LORD says, "In the time of favor I will answer You, and in the day of salvation I will help You" (Isaiah 49:8). Answer and help, back to back. I'd call that a promise worth writing on the oven door.

No test in this verse, friend. The LORD says, "In the time of favor I will answer You, and in the day of salvation I will help You" (Isaiah 49:8). The word is help. The day of salvation comes with the LORD's help.

Not judge, baker. The LORD says, "In the time of favor I will answer You, and in the day of salvation I will help You" (Isaiah 49:8). The LORD says He'll answer and help. A day of salvation sounds a lot like a day of help.

That's it, baker! The Servant is appointed "to say to the prisoners, 'Come out'" (Isaiah 49:9). Two little words, and the door is open. I know a thing or two about waiting in a dark drawer, so I like those words a LOT.
Opposite direction, friend. The Servant is appointed "to say to the prisoners, 'Come out'" (Isaiah 49:9). The prisoners aren't told to stay. They're told to come out.
No patience speech here, baker. The Servant is appointed "to say to the prisoners, 'Come out'" (Isaiah 49:9). It's a short word to prisoners, and it's about leaving.

Not so, baker. The LORD says, "They will not hunger or thirst, nor will scorching heat or sun beat down on them" (Isaiah 49:10). No hunger and no thirst, and no beating sun either. The walk comes with provision.

Right, baker. The text says, "They will not hunger or thirst, nor will scorching heat or sun beat down on them" (Isaiah 49:10). That follows verse 9, where they feed along the pathways and find pasture on barren hills. They're taken care of the whole way.

You got it, baker! "For He who has compassion on them will guide them and lead them beside springs of water" (Isaiah 49:10). Compassion is what's doing the guiding. A walk next to springs of water sounds like a pretty good way to travel.

No grain fields in this verse, friend. It says, "He who has compassion on them will guide them and lead them beside springs of water" (Isaiah 49:10). Verse 9 does talk about pasture on every barren hill. But the guide leads them to springs of water.

Olive trees don't appear in this passage, baker. The verse says, "He who has compassion on them will guide them and lead them beside springs of water" (Isaiah 49:10). Springs of water are where they're led. I think that sounds like a nice rest stop.

That's right, baker! The LORD says, "Behold, they will come from far away, from the north and from the west, and from the land of Aswan" (Isaiah 49:12). People are on the way, and they're coming from every direction. A full house is on its way.

No storm in this verse, friend. The LORD says, "Behold, they will come from far away, from the north and from the west, and from the land of Aswan" (Isaiah 49:12). What's coming is people. They're coming from far away.

No army and no Babylon here, baker. The LORD says, "Behold, they will come from far away, from the north and from the west, and from the land of Aswan" (Isaiah 49:12). It's a crowd of people coming, from the north, the west and Aswan. The roads in verse 11 are for them.

That's right, baker! The text says, "Shout for joy, O heavens; rejoice, O earth; break forth in song, O mountains! For the LORD has comforted His people" (Isaiah 49:13). The reason is right there after the "For." The LORD has comforted His people, and the whole creation is told to sing.

It's true, friend. The text says, "Shout for joy, O heavens; rejoice, O earth; break forth in song, O mountains! For the LORD has comforted His people" (Isaiah 49:13). The heavens, the earth and the mountains are all told to celebrate. The reason follows the word "For."

Yes, baker! "For the LORD has comforted His people, and He will have compassion on His afflicted ones" (Isaiah 49:13). The word compassion also showed up in verse 10, where He guides them beside springs of water. It's a gentle way to end the passage.

Not anger, friend. "For the LORD has comforted His people, and He will have compassion on His afflicted ones" (Isaiah 49:13). The ones who are afflicted get compassion, and that's why the mountains are singing.

Contempt isn't in this verse, baker. "For the LORD has comforted His people, and He will have compassion on His afflicted ones" (Isaiah 49:13). The afflicted ones get compassion from the LORD, and that's where this passage lands.
